definition: Allocate means to distribute or set aside for a particular purpose.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word allocate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know allocate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Before the voyage, the captain allocated the hold: a third for water, a third for cargo, the rest for spare canvas.
Divide is looser than allocate — the pie is merely sliced into portions, with no slice yet promised to anyone or anything; an allocated slice carries a purpose before the meeting ends.
Earmark goes further than allocate — an allocated share can be reshuffled at the next meeting; an earmarked one is welded to its purpose.

Apportion means to divide something by rule into fair shares — the courtroom and census word, where the formula matters most. Allocate is broader and more practical: a committee can allocate by any reasoning it likes, so long as each portion of the whole ends up matched to a purpose and a recipient.

Assign matches one item, seat, or duty to one recipient — no dividing needed, no larger pool implied. Allocate works on a whole: to allocate is to split a limited pool and hand each portion to a purpose. You assign a locker; you allocate the school's whole bank of them.

Ninety garden beds, one hundred forty applicants.
The committee spent a full evening allocating them: two beds to each family with children, one to each single household, four kept back for the school's science classes.
By nine o'clock every bed had a name attached, and every applicant knew exactly where they stood.
Allocate is the exact word for what the committee did, because allocate means to distribute or set aside for a particular purpose — every share came with a label.
Divide would only tell us the beds were split; allocate tells us each portion was matched to a use and a recipient on purpose.
Allocate is budget-table language — committees, treasurers, quartermasters.
Its mirror in this unit is aggregate: aggregating gathers parts into one total, allocating deals one total out into labeled parts.
Earmark goes narrower and firmer, welding a single share to a single purpose; in casual talk, set aside says it plainly.

When the flood relief warehouse opened, everything arrived at once: cots, bottled water, generators, and volunteers with no instructions.
The coordinator's first act was not to unload a single truck but to chalk lines on the concrete floor.

She then began to allocate what they had — the cots to the north bays for families, the water to the loading side where trucks could reach it, six of the eight generators to the clinic tent, two held back for the kitchens.
Every square meter and every machine ended the morning matched to a purpose, and every volunteer could finally be pointed somewhere.
Supplies kept arriving for a week, but the chalk lines never had to be redrawn.
